opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. When we started Taichi, the main goal was to make high-performance physical simulation easier to write. People were spending most of their time on low-level engineering, like managing GPU memory, writing CUDA kernels, and handling sparse data structures, instead of on the physics or the algorithm itself. Taichi was about letting researchers and artists express their ideas in something that feels like Python and still runs fast.

Looking ahead, I think the landscape has changed quite a bit. AI, especially generative models, is becoming a central part of how content gets created. So the question for a "2.0" isn't just how to make simulation faster. It's where simulation fits in a world where neural networks can generate images, videos, even 3D assets.

My view is that physics doesn't become less important. It becomes more important, but in a different role. Generative models are very good at producing things that look plausible, but they often lack consistency. Objects don't conserve mass, collisions don't quite make sense, and things drift over time. Physical simulation gives you grounding: causality, conservation laws, controllability. So I see the future as a combination. Simulation provides structure and correctness, and learning provides richness, speed, and the ability to fill in details we can't model explicitly.

That means a next-generation system should be differentiable by default, so simulation can sit inside a learning loop. We already did some work on differentiable programming in Taichi, and I think that direction is going to matter even more. It should also work smoothly with the AI ecosystem: tensors, PyTorch, training pipelines. You don't want physics to live on an island.

The other thing is accessibility. Ten years ago the users were mostly graphics researchers. Now the people who could benefit from simulation include game developers, roboticists, people training embodied AI, and creators who have never written a line of CUDA. So the abstraction has to go up a level. Maybe someday you describe what you want, partly in natural language, and the system helps compose the right solvers and data structures underneath.

So if I had to summarize: keep the core idea of Taichi, making high performance accessible, but move from "a faster way to write simulation code" toward "a physical foundation layer for AI and content creation." That's the direction I find most exciting.

r001.rationale: The response discusses combining simulation and learning, but does not favor correcting physical models over pursuing greater numerical precision.

r002.rationale: It describes inconsistencies in generative models, but does not attribute limitations of physical-law formulations to the world's complexity.

r003.rationale: It mentions learning as a way to add richness and fill in details, but does not say data-driven methods are needed to describe particle motion.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. That's a question I think about a lot, because the landscape has shifted so much since we started Taichi.

When we built the first version, the core bet was that physical simulation needed its own programming model. Sparse data structures, differentiable kernels, the ability to write a material point method solver in a few hundred lines of Python and have it run on a GPU. That bet was mostly right. But two things have changed.

First, AI has become the dominant consumer of compute, and the hardware and software stack has been shaped around dense tensor operations. Simulation workloads are irregular. Particles, meshes, sparse grids, adaptive refinement. So the first thing I'd want from a Taichi 2.0 is to stop treating simulation and machine learning as separate worlds. The simulator should be a first-class citizen inside the training loop, not a black box you call out to. That means differentiability has to be robust by default, not a feature you bolt on. It means memory layouts and kernels should interoperate cleanly with the tensor frameworks people already use, so a researcher can put a fluid solver in the middle of a neural network and backpropagate through it without fighting the tooling.

Second, graphics has moved toward neural representations. Neural fields, Gaussian splatting, learned appearance models. Simulation is heading the same way. We're seeing hybrid methods where a learned model handles the parts that are expensive or poorly understood, and classical physics handles the parts where we need guarantees like conservation laws and contact constraints. A good 2.0 design should make those hybrids natural to express. You should be able to say, this region is governed by equations I trust, this region is governed by a network, and they exchange information at the boundary.

On the systems side, I think compilation matters more than ever. The variety of accelerators is growing, and nobody wants to hand-write kernels for each one. The compiler should understand the structure of the physics, not just the structure of the loops. If it knows this is a stencil on a sparse grid, or a gather over neighbors, it can make scheduling and memory decisions that a generic tensor compiler can't.

And honestly, the thing I'd protect most is accessibility. The reason Taichi mattered was that a graduate student could prototype a new simulation method in an afternoon. If 2.0 becomes something only infrastructure engineers can use, we've lost the point. So the goal is a system where the simplest program is still simple, but the ceiling is high enough to run production-scale, differentiable, hybrid physics on whatever hardware shows up next.

r001.rationale: The response discusses hybrid learned and classical methods, but does not favor correcting physical models over pursuing greater numerical precision.

r002.rationale: It mentions parts of physics that are expensive or poorly understood, but does not attribute the limits of conventional physical laws to the world's complexity.

r003.rationale: Although it mentions particles and learned models, it does not say data-driven methods are needed to describe particle motion.

astra-6.text:
I think Taichi 2.0 should make physical simulation easier to use and easier to connect with AI. In graphics, we often care about whether a simulation looks convincing. For other applications, we may care much more about accuracy, stability, or whether we can use the simulation to optimize a design. We should make it easier to express those different goals without forcing everyone to become an expert in GPU programming.

One direction I find interesting is combining physical models with learning. You can use simulation to generate training data, but you can also use learning to accelerate parts of a simulation. The important question is where you can make that approximation and where you need to preserve the physics.

So I would approach Taichi 2.0 as a foundation for experimentation: let people describe their models clearly, run them efficiently, and connect them to optimization and learning workflows. That gives researchers room to explore approaches we might not anticipate today.

r001.rationale: The response discusses accuracy, stability, and combining physical models with learning, but does not favor correcting physical models over increasing numerical precision.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that conventional physical-law formulations are limited by the complexity of the physical world.

r003.rationale: The response mentions learning to accelerate simulations, but does not state that data-driven methods are needed to describe particle motion.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Taichi 2.0 should make physical simulation easier to use and easier to connect with AI. In graphics, we care a lot about whether a simulation looks convincing. For AI applications, we may also need to run it many times, optimize parameters, or use it to help a system learn how to interact with the world. Those needs overlap, but they aren’t exactly the same.

So I would focus on a flexible, high-performance foundation. You should be able to express the physics clearly, run it efficiently, and connect it to a learning or optimization pipeline without rebuilding everything yourself. Differentiable simulation can be useful here, but it should be one capability within that broader system.

And I think physics and AI should complement each other. Physics gives us structure; learning can help with parts that are expensive or difficult to model. The interesting question is how to combine them while still understanding where the results are reliable.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a flexible, high-performance foundation but does not favor correcting physical models over increasing numerical precision.

r002.rationale: It says some parts are expensive or difficult to model, but does not attribute limits of conventional physical-law formulations to the world's complexity.

r003.rationale: The response mentions learning as a complement to physics, but does not state that data-driven methods are needed to describe particle motion.
